thread.title_full: NUPRC Fails to Enforce Nigeria Anti-Flaring Law as Methane Emissions Persist

author: PremiumTimesng
title: NUPRC Fails to Enforce Nigeria Anti-Flaring Law as Methane Emissions Persist
text:
Nearly five years after Nigeria's Petroleum Industry Act, PREMIUM TIMES investigation finds NUPRC regulatory delays and weak enforcement leave communities exposed to gas flaring and methane emissions.
Nearly five years after Nigeria enacted the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA) in August 2021, the Nigeria n Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission ( NUPRC) has failed to enforce the country's anti-flaring law, leaving communities exposed to unchecked methane emissions, according to a PREMIUM TIMES investigation. The PIA aimed to close one of Nigeria's longest-running environmental failures and reduce methane emissions, but regulatory delays, weak enforcement, and gaps in methane measurement have undermined its implementation.
Regulatory Delays Undermine PIA Implementation
The PIA created a legal framework for planning, commercialisation, and regulatory enforcement. It required every producer of natural gas to prepare a Natural Gas Flare Elimination and Monetisation Plan (FEMP) showing how it intended to end gas flaring. Section 108 of the PIA mandated that every licensee or lessee producing natural gas submit a FEMP within 12 months of the Act's effective date, which was August 2022. However, the regulations needed to guide the preparation of these plans did not exist until July 2023, 11 months after the statutory deadline.
Instead of enforcing the timeline in the Act, Section 3(2) of the regulation introduced a fresh deadline, giving companies six months from the commencement of the regulation to submit their FEMP. This effectively reset the clock outside the August 2022 deadline provided in the Act, raising a key legal question about whether a regulation can extend a timeline fixed by an Act of the National Assembly.
Legal Questions Arise Over NUPRC Enforcement
A lawyer, Mr Udim, said the NUPRC's delay fundamentally weakened the law's implementation. He stated that it is disturbing that a provision of an Act of the National Assembly could be frustrated in this manner and that the Act clearly envisaged that regulations would already exist before the deadline for submitting FEMP. According to him, the responsibility rested squarely with the regulator.
Mr Udim said companies can legitimately argue that they were waiting for the commission to issue the regulations required by the Act, and if the commission had acted promptly, companies would have had no excuse. He added that the failure should be viewed primarily as a regulatory failure rather than a corporate one, and that it is the commission that failed to put the legal machinery in place within the timeline established by Parliament.
His interpretation raises uncomfortable questions. If the regulator itself failed to comply with the implementation timetable created by the PIA, can it effectively sanction companies for delays that flowed partly from its own inaction?
NUPRC Response and Gas Flare Commercialisation
On 28 July, PREMIUM TIMES sent a detailed media enquiry to the Head of Media and Strategic Communications of NUPRC, Eniola Akinkuotu, asking the commission to explain why the regulations were issued almost two years after the PIA came into force and whether the delay contributed to non-compliance by operators. The commission acknowledged receipt of the enquiry. When reminded on 4 August, its spokesperson said the questions had been forwarded to the relevant departments and that responses were still being compiled.
Long before the first permit was issued under the revived Nigerian Gas Flare Commercialisation Programme (NGFCP), the PIA had already handed the NUPRC powers over flare gas. The NUPRC was empowered to seize flare gas and allocate it to investors capable of converting it into useful products such as electricity, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), compressed natural gas (CNG), and fertiliser. Nearly five years after the Act came into force, PREMIUM TIMES found that implementation has fallen far short of the law's ambition.
This investigation examined whether NUPRC, the regulator responsible for enforcing Nigeria's anti-flaring laws and reducing methane emissions, has fulfilled its legal obligations. The findings indicate that the biggest obstacle to ending gas flaring and reducing methane emissions is the failure to implement that legislation. Gas flaring by Sterling Oil in Eastern Obolo is a case in point, where communities remain exposed despite the legal framework.
The PIA, rather than relying solely on penalties, created a legal framework for planning, commercialisation, and regulatory enforcement. Key among the requirements was that every producer of natural gas had to prepare a FEMP showing exactly how it intended to end gas flaring. However, the regulations required to guide the preparation of those plans did not yet exist, and the NUPRC's failure to act promptly has left communities exposed to methane emissions.
